chunks: In the narration of Muhammad ibn Qays, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), he said:

The Commander of the Believers (peace be upon him) ruled regarding four persons who peered into a pit dug for a lion, so one of them fell and grabbed hold of the second, and the second grabbed hold of the third, and the third grabbed hold of the fourth, until they dragged each other down upon the lion and the lion killed them all.

So he (AS) ruled that the first was the prey of the lion, and imposed upon his family one-third of the blood money (diyah) to the family of the second; imposed upon the family of the second two-thirds of the blood money to the family of the third; and imposed upon the third a complete blood money to the family of the fourth.

key_terms.الدِّيَة: Diyah (blood money): the financial compensation paid to victims' families in cases of homicide
key_terms.زُبْيَة: A pit or trench dug as a trap for wild animals, typically covered or concealed
key_terms.غَرَّمَ: To impose a financial penalty or liability; to hold someone responsible for compensation
key_terms.فَرِيسَة: Prey; in legal usage, a victim treated as having been killed directly by an animal with no human liability
key_terms.قَضَى: To render a legal judgment or judicial ruling; a technical term for the act of judicial decision-making

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on diyah (blood money) when multiple people fall into a pit and kill each other?
ai.summary: This hadith preserves a legal ruling (qadha') of Imam Ali (AS), narrated through Imam al-Baqir (AS), concerning a remarkable chain-liability scenario. Four men peered into a lion trap and fell in a cascade — each grabbing the one below them — and all were killed by the lion. The Imam's ruling assigned graduated diyah liability: the first was treated as pure lion-prey (no human liability for his own death), while each subsequent victim's family received increasing fractions of diyah from those who caused their fall above them. The ruling demonstrates the Shia jurisprudential principle of proportional causation (tasabbub) in wrongful death, where the degree of one's culpability scales with one's causal contribution to another's death.
